analysis.one_liner: Requires nursing homes to report COVID-19 infections, deaths, and resident demographics publicly.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in two House committees until the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: During the COVID-19 pandemic, nursing homes were required by federal regulation to report infections, deaths, and preparedness information, but that rule could be changed without Congress. This bill would write that requirement into law so it could not be quietly dropped, and would require the government to publish state-level breakdowns of who got sick and died in nursing homes — by age, race and ethnicity, and language — on the public Nursing Home Compare website. It died in committee without ever being considered.
analysis.who_benefits: Families trying to choose a nursing home during the pandemic, residents and their advocates, and the low-wage workers inside these facilities, all of whom would get a public, legally required accounting of infections and deaths. Researchers and journalists tracking the disproportionate toll on older, minority, and non-English-speaking residents would also gain.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nursing home residents, their families, and workers

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it a statutory requirement that long-term care facilities report the COVID-19 preparedness, testing, infection, and death data described in the existing federal regulation 42 CFR 483.80(g), so the reporting obligation is locked in by law rather than resting on a regulation the agency could revise [S2] [S3].

The Secretary of Health and Human Services must post state-level demographic data — age, race/ethnicity, and preferred language — for residents with COVID-19 infections and for residents who died, on the public Nursing Home Compare website [S2] [S3].
Any information made public must be released in a way that protects the identity of individual residents [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Nursing home and long-term care operators, who would carry the ongoing reporting burden and face public disclosure of infection and death figures that could damage their reputations and standing with regulators and referral sources.
analysis.who_pays_short: Nursing home and long-term care operators

drawbacks.text: The bill largely writes an existing regulation into law rather than adding new duties, so its practical effect in the middle of a pandemic was limited — the reporting obligation it enforces was already in the Code of Federal Regulations [S2] [S3].

Facilities already strained by the pandemic would bear the cost of collecting and reporting the data, and publicized infection and death counts could penalize facilities that serve the hardest-hit populations.

The demographic data is published only aggregated by state, not per facility, so families comparing specific homes would get less from this bill than the facility-level data already on Nursing Home Compare [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is real but modest: the bill entrenches a reporting requirement that already existed and adds public state-level demographic breakdowns, at the cost of a compliance burden on facilities. It is a transparency measure, not new care standards, staffing rules, or funding — so it would not by itself have improved conditions inside homes.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced, neither committee ever acted on it, and the bill expired when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Steven Horsford introduced the bill on May 13, 2020, and it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee the same day [S1] [S5].
Six House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did [S4].
The action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action after the referral, and the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, killing the bill [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing home operators were better off, because the reporting requirement was never locked into statute and the demographic data was never required to be published. Members of Congress paid no political price, since the bill never reached a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nursing home operators and inactive committees

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken. All six cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on, but no one is recorded as opposing it either.

industries.industry: Nursing home and long-term care operators
industries.note: The bill would have made reporting of COVID-19 infections, deaths, and preparedness data a permanent statutory duty and published state-level demographic breakdowns of who died. Operators benefit when the obligation stays a revisable regulation and the demographic data stays unpublished, and the bill died before either happened.
